web_title: 6. Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: “Our year-to-date performance and customer demand give us confidence to raise our 2026 outlook for the third time this year.” [3]
epigraph.author: Simon Edwards, Chief Financial Officer

web_blocks.text: The financial record shows a business moving from deep cash use to rapid reported growth, with project working capital still central. Revenue was $1,333.470 million in 2023, $1,473.856 million in 2024 and $2,023.994 million in 2025. Product revenue rose to $1,531.281 million in 2025 and accounted for most of the increase; installation grew from $122.318 million to $204.068 million, service from $213.542 million to $228.295 million and electricity from $52.843 million to $60.350 million. The disclosed segment boundary remained one operating segment. [1][4]

web_blocks.caption: Ten-year audited financial trajectory (USD millions except weighted-average shares; cash = cash and cash equivalents, excluding restricted cash; citations identify filing basis) [1][4][5][26][27][28][29][30][31]
web_blocks.takeaway: S-1 rows are pre-IPO as-filed values. The 2019 10-K later revised FY2016-FY2018 revenue/operating results and FY2017-FY2018 cash flows; note below explains the resulting comparability break. Debt is carrying value of current and non-current recourse/non-recourse borrowings, including related-party debt where disclosed; it excludes financing obligations and operating leases. Share counts are the filed basic/diluted weighted-average denominator; early pre-IPO capital bases are not comparable to post-IPO shares.

web_blocks.text: Reported operating cash flow was volatile: negative $372.531 million in 2023, positive $91.998 million in 2024 and positive $113.949 million in 2025. Cash purchases of property, plant and equipment were $83.739 million, $58.852 million and $56.759 million, respectively. The resulting CFO-minus-PPE subtotal was negative $456.270 million, positive $33.146 million and positive $57.190 million. This author-calculated bridge is not Bloom’s defined free-cash-flow measure and excludes investments in unconsolidated affiliates; it is useful because it isolates one recurring cash burden, not because it captures every claim on cash. [1][4]

The 2023 outflow was driven by more than an accounting loss. The annual cash-flow statement shows uses in accounts receivable, contract assets and inventories, alongside operating expense and non-cash adjustments. In 2024, operating cash flow recovered while contract assets and customer deposits moved differently; in 2025 it rose to $113.949 million, helped by working-capital movements including accounts payable and accrued expenses, with contract assets still consuming cash. The year-to-year swing demonstrates why revenue growth alone is an incomplete read-through to self-funding capacity. [1][4]

The first nine months of 2026 produced $3,052.256 million in revenue and $521.523 million in net income, with $272.895 million of operating cash flow. Purchases of PP&E were $231.310 million and investments in unconsolidated affiliates were $26.577 million. CFO less PP&E purchases was therefore $41.585 million before affiliate investment. Reported earnings were much larger than this narrow cash-after-plant subtotal, so you should examine noncash compensation, working capital, customer consideration and financing alongside GAAP income. [2][3]

The working-capital account changes are substantial. At September 30, 2026, current and long-term contract assets totaled $858.646 million, compared with $241.186 million at December 31, 2025; inventory was $927.670 million versus $643.306 million. The 10-Q attributes contract-asset growth primarily to higher volume, project activity and billing milestones. Its nine-month cash-flow statement includes $618.002 million in contract-asset cash use and $264.825 million in accounts-receivable cash use, partly offset by higher accounts payable, accruals and deferred revenue/customer deposits. Acceptance and billing milestones are therefore essential cash-conversion KPIs. [2]

web_blocks.caption: Year-end billed receivables, contract assets and AR-days proxy (USD millions except days) [1][4][5][27][28][29][30][31]
web_blocks.takeaway: *For each reported value, proxy = 365 × year-end net accounts receivable ÷ same-year revenue. FY2016-FY2017 use S-1 as-filed revenue and receivables and are not comparable to later restated years. Contract assets are not separately reported in the indicated early years; “not separately reported” is not zero.

web_blocks.text: The 2019 10-K explains a retrospective revision that matters for this decade view. S-1 originally reported FY2016/FY2017 revenue of $208.540/$375.996 million and operating losses of $240.983/$157.279 million; the later 10-K revised them to $206.391/$365.623 million and losses of $239.574/$155.072 million. FY2018 was revised from $742.038 million revenue and a $153.857 million operating loss to $632.648 million and a $165.009 million loss. For cash flow, FY2017 CFO/PP&E purchases moved from S-1’s -$67.176/$5.140 million to the later filing’s -$91.966/$61.454 million; FY2018 moved from -$58.417/$14.659 million to -$91.948/$45.205 million. The ten-year table preserves the S-1 original basis for FY2016-FY2017 and uses later restated FY2018 onward values where available. The FY2019 10-K also revised FY2017 stock-based compensation from $30.479 million to $29.101 million; later comparative share denominators differ from the pre-IPO S-1 figures. The table labels these breaks rather than implying a clean comparable series. [5][26][27]

The AR-days measure is a deterministic proxy, not a conventional average-balance DSO: 365 × ending net billed receivables divided by that fiscal year’s revenue. It excludes unbilled contract assets, financing receivables and payment-term differences, so the higher FY2022-FY2023 values and subsequent decline are signals to investigate, not proof of customer delinquency or faster cash collection. Contract assets grew from $25.201 million in FY2021 to $241.186 million in FY2025. By September 30, 2026, billed receivables were $634.743 million and current plus non-current contract assets were $858.646 million; no FY2026 DSO is calculated because the revenue period is only nine months and annualizing it would add an assumption. [1][2][29][30][31]

web_blocks.caption: Accounting invested-capital proxy, not standard after-tax ROIC (USD millions) [1][4][30][31]
web_blocks.takeaway: Proxy = EBIT ÷ average of beginning- and end-year (recourse plus non-recourse debt + total stockholders’ equity including NCI − cash). It excludes leases, financing obligations and redeemable interests; it is pre-tax and is not a company-reported ROIC.

web_blocks.text: The operating return trend is evidence of an inflection, not yet a WACC spread. GAAP EBIT was negative in each year from FY2016 through FY2023, then positive at $22.909 million in FY2024 and $72.802 million in FY2025. The simplified pre-tax proxy is -36.5% in FY2023, 2.8% in FY2024 and 7.8% in FY2025. Because the invested-capital definition changed with project financing and consolidation, and because a normalized after-tax return requires a consistent tax and capital base, those proxies should be treated as directional. A market-derived WACC requires price-sensitive equity inputs; that comparison is reserved for Pass 2, and no WACC is estimated in this price-blind pass. [1][4][30][31]

The balance sheet combined a large cash balance with material debt and financing obligations. At December 31, 2025, cash and equivalents were $2,454.108 million and recourse debt was $2,613.726 million. At September 30, 2026, cash and equivalents were $2,486.702 million and recourse debt was $2,473.499 million. The 2025 cash raise included $2.5 billion principal of 0% convertible notes before related exchange transactions and issuance costs. These balances should be considered with non-recourse project debt, lease obligations, financing liabilities, restricted cash and covenants; cash is not synonymous with unencumbered operating cash generation. [1][2]

The balance sheet also carries historical losses. Accumulated deficit was $3,986.983 million at December 31, 2025 and $3,470.694 million at September 30, 2026, following positive 2026 year-to-date earnings. The company also recognized $157.641 million of stock-based compensation in the first nine months of 2026. That expense is noncash in the period but remains an economic compensation cost and can affect share count over time. The right interpretation is neither to subtract it twice from cash nor to ignore it when comparing GAAP and non-GAAP operating performance. [1][2][3]

Customer concentration affects both revenue quality and collections. FY2025 revenue shares from the largest three customers were approximately 43%, 13% and 12%; the largest was a related party. The 2024 shares were 23%, 16% and 14%, while two customers were 37% and 26% in 2023. The Q3 2026 filing reports significant related-party revenue and receivables; channel and financing structures can make a direct customer different from the end user. You should monitor concentration by invoice customer and, where disclosed, end-use customer, while checking credit losses, billing milestones and customer acceptance. [1][2]

Financial quality improved in the recent period, but a full-cycle verdict needs more proof. The CFO waterfall moved from a large 2023 deficit to modest positive cash after plant purchases in 2024 and 2025. Nine-month 2026 revenue and earnings strengthened, yet the cash-after-PP&E subtotal remained small relative to reported net income and revenue, and contract assets and inventory expanded. Future cash flow will depend on collections, customer deposits, project mix, capacity utilization, warranty experience and debt service. You should follow the same line items over several periods rather than infer durability from a record quarter or an isolated negative quarter. [1][2][3][4]

The right forensic conclusion is two-sided. Bloom has demonstrated meaningful revenue scale, a strong recent product mix, positive recent operating income and increased cash from operations. It has also relied on substantial external financing, carries high customer concentration, has a volatile historical CFO record, and is investing heavily while working capital expands. It is not yet possible to characterize cash generation as mature and self-funding through varying project conditions. The decisive operating test is whether the company converts a broader, delivered installed base into service contribution and cash after necessary plant investment without increasing guarantees or financing dependence. [1][2]

The cash-flow difference is not explained by one line alone. Net income includes noncash adjustments such as stock-based compensation, depreciation and gains or losses. Working-capital movements include cash uses in receivables, contract assets, inventory, prepaid costs and other assets, and cash sources in payables, accruals and deferred customer revenue. The Q3 2026 filing records $157.641 million of stock-based compensation during the first nine months. This is a noncash add-back in CFO, yet still an economic cost to employees and shareholders; it should not be silently removed from a business-quality assessment. [2]

Longer-term balance-sheet comparisons show both funding and exposure. Bloom ended 2025 with $2,454.108 million cash and $2,613.726 million recourse debt after issuing $2.5 billion principal of 0% convertible notes in November 2025 and completing debt exchanges. At September 2026 it had $2,486.702 million cash and $2,473.499 million recourse debt. The Q3 filing also lists non-recourse debt, financing obligations, operating lease liabilities and restricted cash. You should use the full obligation set and financing covenants, not compare cash only with one debt subtotal. [1][2]

The historical waterfall puts the 2026 result in perspective. The 2023 CFO-minus-PP&E subtotal was negative $456.270 million; it was positive $33.146 million in 2024 and $57.190 million in 2025. For the first nine months of 2026, CFO less PP&E purchases was $41.585 million before investments in unconsolidated affiliates. The periods are not identical—three quarters are compared with full years—so do not infer a trend from the raw amounts. You can, however, see that significant growth has not yet produced a large residual after plant investment. [1][2][4]

Customer-level terms affect net sales as well as cash timing. The Q3 filing says share-based consideration promised to a customer’s customer is recorded as customer consideration and reduces revenue as associated systems are delivered. Some arrangements also contain financing, leases, performance warranties and renewal rights. You should trace the accounting across the contract: equipment delivery, service obligation, customer incentives, contract asset, receivable and cash settlement. This makes customer economics more transparent than relying on a single reported gross-margin ratio. [1][2]

The financial watch list for the next period is therefore specific: contract assets converting into invoices and cash; inventory converting into accepted systems; CFO relative to PP&E purchases; debt service and financing costs; product and installation margins; service renewal and guarantees; and top-customer concentration. A sustained improvement across those measures would support the view that the 2026 demand step-up is becoming self-financing. A reversal in one or more of them would identify whether the constraint is customer conversion, installation execution, service quality or capital allocation. [1][2][3]

book_paragraphs: When you analyze Bloom’s financial history, begin with the scale of revenue and then ask how that revenue became cash. Total revenue was $1,333.470 million in FY2023, $1,473.856 million in FY2024 and $2,023.994 million in FY2025. Product revenue was $975.245 million, $1,085.153 million and $1,531.281 million, respectively; installation was $92.796 million, $122.318 million and $204.068 million; service was $183.065 million, $213.542 million and $228.295 million; electricity was $82.364 million, $52.843 million and $60.350 million. You should preserve the one-segment boundary while using the four categories to understand mix. [1][4]

Now inspect the CFO waterfall. Operating cash flow was negative $372.531 million in 2023, positive $91.998 million in 2024 and positive $113.949 million in 2025. Purchases of PP&E were $83.739 million, $58.852 million and $56.759 million. When you subtract those purchases, the calculated subtotal is negative $456.270 million, positive $33.146 million and positive $57.190 million. These exact amounts are CFO less PP&E purchases, not company-reported free cash flow, and they exclude affiliate investments. You should use the subtotal as a transparent bridge rather than give it a corporate label it does not have. [1][4]

The annual pattern gives you a more useful story than revenue alone. In 2023, cash used in accounts receivable, contract assets and inventories contributed to the negative $372.531 million CFO. In 2024 and 2025, CFO turned positive, but project billing and customer deposits still affected the bridge. The 2025 CFO of $113.949 million included favorable movements in accounts payable and accrued expenses, while contract assets used cash. You should therefore ask whether positive CFO reflects cash collected on delivered projects or temporary timing benefits that could reverse as project volume changes. [1][4]

The nine-month 2026 performance accelerated. Revenue reached $3,052.256 million and net income was $521.523 million, while CFO was $272.895 million. PP&E purchases were $231.310 million, leaving $41.585 million after those purchases and before $26.577 million invested in unconsolidated affiliates. You should not call the $41.585 million a full measure of distributable cash; it omits other financing claims and uses an intentionally narrow definition. It still makes the central point: a large net-income figure can coexist with modest residual cash after plant purchases during a rapid factory ramp. [2][3]

Balance-sheet working capital explains much of that gap. Current and long-term contract assets totaled $858.646 million on September 30, 2026, compared with $241.186 million at December 31, 2025. Inventory rose from $643.306 million to $927.670 million. In the nine-month cash-flow statement, contract assets absorbed $618.002 million and accounts receivable absorbed $264.825 million, while payables, accruals and deferred revenue provided offsets. You should connect those balances to customer billing milestones and acceptance. If a system is built but the billing trigger or acceptance event is delayed, revenue, receivable and cash conversion may occur on different timelines. [2]

The company held cash of $2,454.108 million and recourse debt of $2,613.726 million at year-end 2025. At September 2026 it reported cash of $2,486.702 million and recourse debt of $2,473.499 million. The 2025 financing included $2.5 billion principal of 0% convertible notes before related exchanges and costs. You should include the financing in the growth story rather than treating the expansion as entirely self-funded. Also account for non-recourse project debt, lease liabilities, financing obligations, restricted cash and covenants when interpreting the cash balance. [1][2]

Historical losses remain visible in accumulated deficit. At December 2025, it stood at $3,986.983 million; by September 2026 it had narrowed to $3,470.694 million after positive year-to-date earnings. Stock-based compensation was $157.641 million in the first nine months of 2026. That is noncash compensation in the cash-flow reconciliation, but it is not economically costless. You should avoid two mistakes: subtracting a noncash expense again from CFO, and excluding it entirely when comparing reported and adjusted operating results. [1][2][3]

Customer concentration means that the shape of revenue can depend on a few counterparties. Bloom’s top three customers represented about 43%, 13% and 12% of FY2025 revenue; in 2024 the corresponding shares were 23%, 16% and 14%, and in 2023 two customers represented 37% and 26%. You should ask who is the direct customer and who is the final user. A finance partner may purchase equipment on behalf of a customer; a large end user may still matter economically even if it is not the direct invoice recipient. Concentration also affects receivables, project delays and service exposure. [1][2]

The Oracle arrangement illustrates that customer acquisition can have consideration outside a conventional cash discount. Bloom’s Q3 filing says share-based consideration to a customer’s customer is recognized as a reduction of revenue as related systems are delivered. You should include such terms when considering net revenue per contract, while respecting what the filing reports and not inventing an allocation by megawatt. This is one reason the face value of a large procurement arrangement cannot be equated directly with Bloom’s net recognized sales. [2]

The overall business shows clear financial improvement and unresolved questions. The FY2023 CFO deficit was large; FY2024 and FY2025 turned positive; nine-month 2026 earnings and CFO rose substantially. At the same time, after-plant-investment cash remained modest, working capital expanded and customers remained concentrated. You should look for repeated evidence that receivables and contract assets convert promptly, inventory turns into accepted systems, service grows without guarantee expense outpacing it, and production capacity is efficiently used. [1][2][4]

For your next review, carry forward a compact forensic panel: annual revenue by the four reported categories; CFO; PP&E purchases; the CFO-minus-PP&E subtotal; contract assets; inventories; customer concentration; recourse and non-recourse debt; cash; service revenue; warranty and performance-guarantee costs; and accepted versus announced megawatts. Keeping those measures side by side lets you distinguish profitable growth from growth that still needs substantial outside capital. You should expect volatility in quarterly project conversion, but a mature business should eventually show repeatable cash generation after maintenance and factory investment. [1][2][3]

Use the nine-month table as an operating bridge, not a collection of isolated facts. Revenue of $3,052.256 million and net income of $521.523 million were materially higher than the comparable 2025 period, when revenue was $1,246.311 million and net loss was $88.566 million. CFO was $272.895 million versus negative $304.124 million, but PP&E purchases increased to $231.310 million from $33.805 million. Contract assets reached $858.646 million and inventory $927.670 million at September 30, 2026. You should see both acceleration and investment demands in the same panel. [2][3]

The most visible gap is between earnings and the cash that remains after factory spending. Nine-month CFO of $272.895 million less PP&E purchases of $231.310 million leaves $41.585 million before the $26.577 million investment in affiliates. This calculation is deliberately narrow and is not a company-defined FCF figure. You should use it to ask whether working capital and capacity investment are being funded by operations, not to label the company permanently cash-generative or cash-consuming on the basis of one nine-month period. [2]

The balance-sheet comparison is similarly mixed. Cash was $2,454.108 million and recourse debt $2,613.726 million at year-end 2025; by September 2026, cash was $2,486.702 million and recourse debt $2,473.499 million. The 2025 convertible financing supported capacity and liquidity but did not eliminate project obligations. You should add financing obligations, operating leases, non-recourse debt, restricted cash and credit covenants to the analysis. A cash balance can protect a growth plan, while the debt structure affects flexibility if customers delay orders or if capital markets tighten. [1][2]

Contract assets and inventory show where growth is being funded. Contract assets rose from $241.186 million at December 31, 2025 to $858.646 million at September 30, 2026; inventory rose from $643.306 million to $927.670 million. The filing links contract assets to project activity, revenue volume and billing milestones. You should ask which balances are awaiting milestones or acceptance, how quickly they convert to receivables, and how much inventory is specific to customer orders versus planned capacity. That is how you distinguish healthy growth investment from a cash-conversion problem. [2]

Noncash expense needs its own lens. Bloom reported $157.641 million of stock-based compensation in the first nine months of 2026. The cash-flow statement adds it back because it is not a period cash payment, but it still compensates employees and may affect ownership over time. You should not use non-GAAP adjustments to erase it from your view of economic costs. At the same time, you should not double-count it as a cash outflow when reconciling CFO. Keep the income-statement expense and cash-flow reconciliation in their correct places. [2][3]

Return to the three-year cash waterfall. In FY2023, CFO was negative $372.531 million and PP&E purchases were $83.739 million, leaving a CFO-minus-PP&E subtotal of negative $456.270 million. FY2024 CFO was $91.998 million, PP&E purchases $58.852 million and subtotal $33.146 million. FY2025 CFO was $113.949 million, PP&E purchases $56.759 million and subtotal $57.190 million. These are calculated subtotals and exclude affiliate investments. You should read them with changing working capital and financing activities, not as polished measures of shareholder cash flow. [1][4]

Customer concentration further qualifies the financial result. In FY2025, the largest three customers represented approximately 43%, 13% and 12% of revenue; in FY2024 they represented 23%, 16% and 14%; and in FY2023 two customers accounted for 37% and 26%. That pattern can create large swings when a financer or strategic partner changes purchasing pace. You should monitor receivables and revenue concentration together, and separate direct invoice concentration from ultimate end-user diversification when the filings allow. [1]

The mix shift toward product makes gross-margin quality important. Q3 2026 product margin was 37.9%, service 17.8%, electricity 25.7%, and installation negative 4.8%; overall gross margin was 33.8%. These values are one quarter and reflect a particular project mix. You should ask whether product margins withstand input-cost pressure, whether installation reaches break-even as standards improve, and whether service remains profitable after guarantees and maintenance. An equipment margin is not a full-fleet margin until service costs and warranty outcomes mature. [3]

The financial story is therefore not complete at “reported profit.” Bloom has moved from large operating cash use in 2023 to positive CFO in 2024 and 2025, and strong earnings and cash flow in the first nine months of 2026. It has also enlarged its working-capital balances and invested heavily in factory assets while remaining concentrated among large customers. You should require several periods of customer collection and post-capex cash generation before describing the model as self-funding through a cycle. [1][2][4]

You now have a decade-long view, but not a perfectly continuous series. Bloom’s S-1 covers its private-era FY2016–FY2017 statements; the 2019 10-K later revised 2016–2018 revenue and operating results, so the table labels the early basis and gives the restated figures. The reported weighted-average share base grew from 53.268 million in FY2018 to 240.402 million in FY2025, while IPO conversion and pre-IPO capital structure make the early share figures non-comparable to simple dilution. Stock-based compensation ranged from $28.157 million in FY2016 to $139.406 million in FY2025, with a high $196.291 million in FY2019. You should treat that expense as compensation, not cash CapEx. [1][5][26][27]

For working capital, the proxy is 365 times year-end billed receivables divided by same-year revenue; it excludes contract assets. The proxy was 93.3 days in FY2023 and 67.0 days in FY2025, while contract assets rose from $41.366 million to $241.186 million. A simple pre-tax return proxy was negative in FY2023, then 2.8% and 7.8% in FY2024 and FY2025. You cannot conclude that returns exceed WACC: a standard after-tax ROIC needs consistent invested-capital and tax treatment, and market-derived WACC requires price-sensitive inputs reserved for Pass 2. [1][2][4][31]

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: You have seen the central accounting tension: reported earnings and revenue can rise quickly while the business still absorbs cash in contract assets, inventory and factory investment. The cash-flow waterfall gives you a transparent measure, but it is only one subtotal. Your discipline is to reconcile profit, working capital, capital spending, customer concentration and financing over several years. Do not declare a durable cash engine until the systems are delivered, accepted, serviced and paid for across more than one demand cycle.
